title: Air India and IndiGo Cut Europe Flights as Winter Capacity Falls 6.5% — and Foreign Carriers Take the Passengers
headline: Air India and IndiGo Cut Europe Flights as Winter Capacity Falls 6.5% — and Foreign Carriers Take the Passengers
subheadline: Air India ends Delhi-Vienna and its Birmingham services and IndiGo has suspended Manchester and will pause Heathrow, as India-Europe winter seats fall to 5.63 million; longer routings around closed airspace and high fuel costs are driving the cuts.
body:
• Air India is cutting four European routes in the winter schedule, including Delhi-Vienna (ending October 31) and its Birmingham services, and has already reduced Delhi-Paris, Delhi-Milan, Delhi-Zurich and Delhi-Rome capacity.
  • IndiGo suspended Delhi-Manchester and Mumbai-Manchester on August 31, will temporarily suspend London Heathrow when its Norse Atlantic damp lease ends, and cuts Mumbai-Amsterdam to three flights a week on the A321XLR.
  • India-Europe winter capacity is 5.63 million two-way seats, down 6.5% from 6.02 million a year earlier, on OAG data cited by Aviation Week — before the latest Air India cuts.
  • If you are flying India-Europe this winter, expect fewer nonstops and higher loads on the remaining ones; compare one-stop options via hub carriers early.

India's two biggest airlines are retreating from Europe at the same time, and the passengers they leave behind are being picked up by foreign carriers. Air India has cut four European routes as winter schedule changes take effect, while IndiGo has scaled back its European network after ending its damp-lease arrangement with Norse Atlantic Airways, according to Live From A Lounge.

What is being cut

"India-Europe winter capacity is 5.63 million two-way seats, down 6.5% from 6.02 million a year earlier, on OAG data cited by Aviation Week — before the latest Air India cuts."

Air India's four-times-weekly Delhi-Vienna service ends on October 31 — ending the only nonstop link between Austria and India — and its three-times-weekly Delhi-Birmingham flights stop on November 1, with Amritsar-Birmingham also pausing for the season. The airline had planned to grow Birmingham by nearly 34 per cent this winter before reversing course. It has already reduced capacity on Delhi-Paris, Delhi-Milan, Delhi-Zurich and Delhi-Rome, and changed services to North America and Australia.

IndiGo suspended flights between Delhi and Manchester and between Mumbai and Manchester on August 31, citing international airspace restrictions, longer flight durations and a difficult operating-cost environment. Its six Boeing 787-9 damp lease with Norse Atlantic concludes around October 25; London Heathrow services will temporarily suspend pending the arrival of IndiGo's own Airbus A350-900 aircraft, at least 12 months away. Mumbai-Amsterdam continues from October 25 on a 195-seat Airbus A321XLR, reduced to three times a week, according to Aviation A2Z.

Why: airspace, fuel and thin margins

The continued closure of Pakistani airspace forces westbound flights onto longer routings that burn more fuel — a penalty that compounds across a winter schedule. Longer routings also mean fewer aircraft rotations, tighter crew duty limits and harder maintenance planning. The demand did not collapse: about 173,500 passengers flew between Vienna and Indian cities in 2025, up 11 per cent, and Birmingham-India carried about 207,300 two-way passengers, down 8.3 per cent. Fuel economics won the argument anyway.

Across the market, airlines scheduled about 5.63 million two-way seats between India and Europe for winter 2026-27, down 6.5% from 6.02 million a year earlier, on OAG data cited by Aviation Week — figures that predate the latest Air India changes, so the final cut is deeper.

What it means for travellers

Every nonstop withdrawn pushes passengers onto one-stop itineraries through Gulf and European hubs — which is precisely how Air India and IndiGo's losses become European and Gulf carriers' gains, as Firstpost's analysis put it. For diaspora families travelling for Diwali, weddings and Christmas, the practical advice is to book the remaining nonstops early, treat Vienna and Birmingham routings as hub connections from now on, and check whether an existing booking has been re-routed before you travel. Air India is still adding capacity elsewhere, including toward Osaka and Sydney on some reports — this is a Europe-specific retrenchment, not a network-wide shrink.
